strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in visual robotic RL: obtaining dense rewards from action-free demonstration videos, reducing reliance on hand-engineered dense rewards and action annotations.

The proposed TimeRewarder method is simple and plausible: predicting normalized temporal distances between frame pairs, using reverse-ordered pairs as implicit negatives, emphasizing short temporal intervals, and using two-hot discretization to stabilize training. The design is easy to understand and integrate with an off-the-shelf RL algorithm.

The empirical evaluation is comparatively broad for this problem setting: 10 Meta-World tasks, eight seeds, multiple progress-based and imitation-from-observation baselines, privileged references, held-out trajectory VOC analysis, qualitative reward/value diagnostics, ablations, and a small cross-domain human-video experiment.

The results are strong in the reported setting. TimeRewarder substantially improves downstream DrQ-v2 learning and often exceeds the Meta-World dense reward reference, and the ablations support the usefulness of implicit negatives, weighted sampling, and discretization.
Reproducibility is partly supported by clear equations, model description, task list, and key hyperparameters for reward learning and RL.
weaknesses: The main claims are somewhat overstated because the best RL results combine the learned proxy reward with a sparse environment success signal. Appendix results without this sparse reward report no full successes within the short training budget, which weakens the claim that TimeRewarder alone provides sufficient reward for task completion.

The theoretical justification is weak. It mostly argues that temporal distance can correspond to progress along optimal expert trajectories under strong assumptions; it does not establish that the learned frame-pair predictor will assign reliable rewards to off-expert or causally suboptimal states encountered during RL.

The method’s robustness to non-monotonic tasks is limited. The conclusion briefly mentions frequent back-and-forth motions, but the paper does not deeply analyze failure modes where temporal order is a poor proxy for task progress, where multiple valid solution modes exist, or where demonstrations contain pauses, retries, or variable-speed behavior.

The comparison to the hand-designed environment dense reward is potentially misleading. Surpassing the Meta-World reward does not necessarily imply a generally better reward; it may reflect reward scaling, interaction with DrQ-v2, or poor tuning of the dense reward baseline. More calibration and sensitivity analysis would make this claim safer.

Some experimental details remain underspecified for full reproducibility, including exact environment initialization ranges, image preprocessing, augmentation, sparse reward weight alpha, baseline-specific tuning, demonstration generation protocol, and whether code/data will be released. The project page field appears blank in the extracted manuscript.

The cross-domain human-video experiment is promising but small: only three tasks, with one in-domain video plus 20 human videos, and limited analysis of viewpoint, embodiment, or background confounds. It supports feasibility more than broad cross-domain generalization.

Originality is moderate rather than high. The method is a useful synthesis of temporal ranking/progress reward learning ideas, but the core idea of using temporal structure in demonstrations as reward supervision is closely related to VIP, Rank2Reward, PROGRESSOR, TCN-style methods, and value/order learning from videos.

There is no meaningful ethics or broader-impact discussion despite the robotics setting. The risks of learned visual rewards, reward hacking, unsafe exploration, and deploying proxy rewards outside the training distribution deserve more explicit treatment.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: learning dense rewards for visual RL from action-free videos, reducing dependence on manually engineered task rewards and action-labeled demonstrations.

The proposed method is simple and plausible: predicting signed temporal distances between pairs of demonstration frames gives an intuitive progress signal, and the weighted pair sampling, reverse-order negatives, and two-hot discretization are reasonable design choices.

The empirical evaluation is broader than many papers in this area: 10 Meta-World tasks, multiple baselines, eight seeds, ablations of key components, and an additional cross-domain experiment using human videos on three tasks.

The results, if reproduced, suggest strong practical utility in the tested setting, with TimeRewarder improving sample efficiency and final success over several imitation-from-observation and progress-based reward baselines.

The appendix provides some useful implementation details, including model backbone, reward-model training hyperparameters, RL hyperparameters, task list, and additional VIP backbone and proxy-only reward experiments.
weaknesses: The main claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The primary RL results combine the learned proxy reward with a sparse environment success signal, while the appendix experiment without sparse reward reports no full task successes within the training budget. This substantially weakens the claim that the method by itself supplies sufficient dense reward from passive videos.

The novelty is limited. The work is close to existing temporal-progress and rank/order-based reward learning methods such as VIP, Rank2Reward, PROGRESSOR, TCN-style temporal learning, and potential-based shaping. The paper does not clearly establish why signed temporal-distance prediction is a major conceptual advance rather than a useful incremental variant.

The theoretical justification is weak. It relies on expert optimality, monotonic progress, uniform per-step costs, and goal-directed trajectories; these assumptions are exactly where many manipulation tasks with backtracking, retries, contacts, or non-monotonic motions become difficult. The derivation does not justify generalization to failed or out-of-distribution agent rollouts.

The comparison to environment dense rewards is hard to interpret. The paper claims to outperform manually designed dense rewards, but does not sufficiently analyze whether this comes from reward scaling, reward mixing with sparse success, DrQ-v2 tuning, different optimization difficulty, or the quality of Meta-World dense rewards. Calling the dense reward an upper bound is also questionable.

The cross-domain evidence is promising but narrow. It covers only three tasks, still trains and evaluates policies in Meta-World rather than on real robots, and uses only 20 human videos plus one in-domain simulation demonstration. This does not yet support broad claims about scalable learning from in-the-wild or real-world human videos.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important details are missing or underreported, including the sparse-reward weight alpha, preprocessing and augmentation, image resolution, exact CLIP initialization and fine-tuning protocol, evaluation frequency, baseline hyperparameter tuning, demonstration-generation protocol, randomization ranges, and whether code/data will be released.

The visual-only figures make several quantitative claims difficult to verify. The paper would benefit from tables of final success rates, confidence intervals, sample-efficiency metrics, and statistical tests rather than relying mainly on dense curve plots.

The ablations support the components qualitatively, but the analysis is largely post hoc. Several explanations, such as why discretization preserves sharp transitions or why reverse pairs simulate suboptimal behavior, are plausible but not rigorously validated.

The method has an important structural limitation: it assumes temporal order in successful demonstrations is a reliable proxy for task progress. The paper acknowledges difficulty with back-and-forth motions only briefly, but this limitation could affect many realistic tasks with exploration, retries, reversible subtasks, or multiple valid strategies.

The paper lacks an adequate ethics and limitations discussion. Learning affect-free robotic reward models from human videos raises consent, privacy, dataset provenance, misuse, and deployment-safety issues, and these are not meaningfully addressed.

strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and practically useful: predicting normalized temporal distance between video frames gives a dense progress reward from action-free demonstrations. The formulation is easy to understand and integrates cleanly with standard visual RL.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad for this problem setting: 10 Meta-World tasks, comparison to progress-based reward learning, ILfO, and privileged dense-reward/BC references, plus mean and standard deviation over eight seeds. TimeRewarder is consistently strong, reportedly best on 9/10 tasks and often more sample-efficient than the baselines.

The paper includes useful diagnostic evaluations beyond final success rate, including value-order correlation on held-out expert videos, qualitative success/failure reward curves, ablations of implicit negative sampling, weighted sampling, discretization, and alternative temporal modeling designs.

The cross-domain experiment with human videos is a promising addition. Even though limited to three tasks, the result that 20 unlabeled human videos plus one in-domain demo improves over either source alone supports the broader motivation of leveraging passive video data.
weaknesses: The central scalability claims are stronger than the evidence. Most results use 100 scripted Meta-World demonstrations per task and still rely on a sparse binary success signal during RL. The appendix experiment without sparse success signals reports no successful completions within 200k frames, which weakens claims that the learned proxy reward alone is sufficient for task acquisition.

The theoretical justification is quite limited. It assumes expert optimality, approximately constant per-step costs, monotonic progress, and gamma close to 1, which makes temporal distance align with progress mostly by construction. It does not address common manipulation cases with pauses, retries, non-monotonic motions, or multiple valid strategies except for a brief concluding limitation.

The argument that reverse-ordered expert frame pairs provide suboptimal-awareness is not fully convincing. Backward transitions along an expert trajectory are not the same distribution as real failed exploration states, contacts, stalls, or visually plausible but causally wrong actions. Figure 4 is helpful but anecdotal, using only selected trajectories for two tasks.

The empirical scope remains simulation-heavy. The human-video study uses real videos only for reward learning while policy learning and evaluation remain in Meta-World copies, so the paper does not demonstrate real-robot transfer or robustness to richer real-world nuisances.

Presentation and reproducibility are adequate but incomplete. Hyperparameters and task lists are provided, but implementation details for baselines, reward scaling/alpha selection, computational cost, dataset release/code availability, and statistical testing are not sufficiently detailed to fully assess reproducibility. The project page field appears blank in the manuscript.

Limitations and ethics are underdeveloped. The paper briefly mentions back-and-forth motions as a limitation, but does not discuss failure modes such as reward hacking, misuse of human videos/consent, privacy in passive video collection, or safety risks from learned rewards in robotic deployment.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple and well-motivated reward-learning objective: predicting signed temporal distance between video frames and using adjacent-frame predictions as dense RL rewards. The method is easy to understand and directly targets a real bottleneck in visual robotic RL from action-free demonstrations.

The empirical section is fairly strong for a simulated robotics paper. It compares against multiple relevant progress-based and ILfO baselines, uses 10 Meta-World tasks, reports mean and standard deviation over eight seeds, and includes ablations for negative sampling, weighted sampling, discretization, and alternative temporal modeling choices.

The paper makes a useful effort to analyze behavior beyond final success rates, including value-order correlation on held-out demonstrations, qualitative reward/value curves on failed versus successful rollouts, PCA visualizations, human-video transfer experiments, and an additional ManiSkill task in the appendix.

Presentation is clear overall. The method, training target, reward use, and implementation details are described cleanly, and the appendix includes hyperparameters and several extra comparisons that improve interpretability.

The limitations around single-frame ambiguity and back-and-forth motions are acknowledged explicitly, and the paper gives a plausible direction for history-based extensions rather than hiding the issue.
weaknesses: The central claim is somewhat overstated because the main RL experiments combine the learned proxy reward with an environment-provided sparse success signal. The appendix shows that using only the learned proxy reward yields no successes within the same short training budget, which materially weakens the impression that TimeRewarder alone solves reward learning from passive videos.

Originality is moderate rather than high. The work is a clean signed-distance variant in a crowded line of temporal-progress reward learning methods, closely related to Rank2Reward, PROGRESSOR, VIP, TCC/TCN-style temporal supervision, and potential-based progress shaping. The novelty is useful, but not conceptually deep.

The theoretical justification relies on very restrictive assumptions: deterministic fully observable MDPs, optimal expert trajectories, unique visual state identification, no cyclic/aliased observations, and temporal distance as a monotonic proxy for value. These assumptions do not cover many realistic manipulation settings, and the paper’s own discussion notes important violations.

The experimental evidence is still mostly simulation-based and concentrated in Meta-World with scripted demonstrations. The human-video experiments are promising but limited to three tasks, require at least one in-domain Meta-World demonstration, and do not evaluate real-robot policy learning.

The comparison to environment dense rewards is hard to interpret. TimeRewarder plus sparse success sometimes outperforming hand-designed dense rewards may reflect deficiencies of Meta-World rewards or reward-scale choices rather than a general superiority of learned progress rewards.

Reproducibility is adequate but incomplete. Hyperparameters are provided, but there is no clear code or dataset release statement in the manuscript, and some important setup details such as broadened initialization ranges, adaptive alpha selection, human-video collection protocol, and baseline tuning could be specified more precisely.

The ethics/impact discussion is generic. Since the method learns robotic rewards from human videos, the paper should more concretely discuss consent/privacy for collected videos, potential misuse in robotic manipulation, and failure modes from misinterpreting passive demonstrations.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: reducing manual dense-reward engineering for visual robotic RL from action-free videos.
The proposed method is simple and clearly motivated: train a pairwise visual model to predict signed temporal distance between frames, then use adjacent-frame progress as a dense proxy reward.

The empirical section is reasonably broad within simulation, covering 10 Meta-World tasks, several progress-based and imitation-from-observation baselines, eight seeds, ablations, and one additional ManiSkill task in the appendix.

The paper includes useful diagnostics beyond final success rate, such as value-order correlation, reward/value curve visualizations, representation plots, and ablations for negative sampling, weighted pair sampling, discretization, input form, and order prediction.
The cross-domain experiment with human videos is a promising direction and suggests the approach may benefit from heterogeneous passive videos.
weaknesses: The central claim is overstated because the main RL results still combine TimeRewarder with an online sparse success reward. The appendix reports that using only the learned proxy reward achieves no task successes within the same short training budget, which substantially weakens claims about learning dense rewards from passive videos alone.

Originality is limited. The method is essentially supervised temporal-distance prediction over demonstration frame pairs with reverse pairs and biased sampling. This is a natural variant of prior progress/order/value learning methods such as VIP, Rank2Reward, PROGRESSOR, TCC-style temporal learning, and arrow-of-time objectives, and the paper does not make a strong conceptual case for why this particular formulation is a major advance.

The theoretical justification is too idealized to support the broad claims. It assumes deterministic fully observable MDPs, optimal expert trajectories, a single monotonic route to the goal, and observations that identify task phase. The paper itself notes that visual aliasing and back-and-forth motions break these assumptions, but the proposed fix of using histories is not implemented or evaluated.

The interpretation of reverse-ordered expert pairs as 'implicit negative sampling' is not fully convincing. Reverse temporal labels do not necessarily model the distribution of suboptimal online behavior, failed contact, loops, distractor motion, or irreversible dynamics; nevertheless the paper makes strong claims about suboptimality awareness and causally grounded feedback.

The evaluation is narrower than the motivation suggests. Most evidence is in Meta-World simulation with scripted demonstrations and visual observations, plus one simple ManiSkill task. There is no real robot experiment, no downstream evaluation of policies trained from human videos on real hardware, and limited evidence for robustness to camera changes, distractors, non-expert videos, multi-stage tasks, or cyclic tasks.

The comparison to the environment dense reward is potentially misleading. The paper claims to outperform manually designed dense rewards, but the learned reward is trained from 100 successful demonstrations and is also combined with sparse success signals; this is not an apples-to-apples replacement for the environment reward baseline.

Several experimental details needed for reproducibility are missing or under-specified, including code/data release status, exact expanded initialization ranges, human-video collection protocol, preprocessing, frame sampling rates, baseline-specific tuning, reward normalization details, and how the adaptive alpha is computed and applied across methods.

The visual evidence is sometimes qualitative and selectively chosen, especially the successful/failed trajectory plots and representation PCA. These figures are useful but do not substitute for systematic failure analysis across many failed rollouts.

Limitations and ethics are minimal. The paper acknowledges POMDP/cyclic-motion issues but does not deeply analyze safety risks from reward hacking, failures under visual aliasing, use of VLM/human success annotation, or the consequences of deploying learned rewards in real robotic systems.

Presentation overclaims in several places, especially phrases implying reward learning free of manually engineered rewards or action annotations, robust progress scoring, and scalable watch-to-act learning from in-the-wild videos. The evidence supports a narrower claim: temporal-distance supervision can be an effective auxiliary dense reward in simulated tasks when paired with sparse success feedback.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple and well-motivated reward learning objective: predict signed frame-wise temporal distance from passive videos and use adjacent-frame predictions as dense RL rewards. The formulation is clean, easy to understand, and connects naturally to progress-based reward shaping.

Empirical evaluation is broad and convincing for the chosen setting. The paper evaluates on 10 Meta-World manipulation tasks, compares against several relevant progress-based and ILfO baselines, reports mean and standard deviation over eight seeds, and shows strong downstream RL gains in both final success and sample efficiency.

The ablations are unusually useful. The authors isolate implicit negative sampling, weighted pair sampling, two-hot discretization, and alternative temporal modeling choices, and the results support the claim that signed temporal distance modeling is doing meaningful work rather than merely benefiting from a strong visual backbone.

The manuscript makes a good effort to test generalization: held-out expert trajectories, failed rollout analysis, representation visualizations, cross-domain human-video augmentation on three tasks, a ManiSkill task in the appendix, VIP backbone controls, from-scratch backbone experiments, and additional OT baselines.

Presentation is clear overall. The method is compact, figures are informative, implementation hyperparameters are provided, and the limitations around visual aliasing/back-and-forth motions are acknowledged rather than hidden.

The contribution is practically significant: learning dense rewards from action-free videos is important for robotics, and the method is substantially simpler than several prior pipelines while performing strongly in sparse-reward visual RL experiments.
weaknesses: The central claims are somewhat stronger than the evidence permits. The method is described as learning from passive videos and reducing manual reward engineering, but the main RL results still combine the learned reward with an environment sparse success signal. Appendix results without sparse success signals show no full successes within the short training budget, which materially qualifies the headline claim.

The theoretical justification is limited. It assumes deterministic fully observable MDPs, optimal expert trajectories, monotonic progress, and reconstructability of state from a single observation. These assumptions exclude exactly the cyclic, visually aliased, and non-monotone behaviors that often occur in manipulation, so the theory is best viewed as intuition rather than a robust guarantee.

Real-world evidence remains preliminary. Human videos are used only as reward-learning data to improve simulated Meta-World RL, and only on three tasks. There is no real-robot policy learning or deployment, so claims about scalable watch-to-act robot learning should be tempered.

The method may be sensitive to demonstration structure. It learns temporal distance as progress, so demonstrations with pauses, retries, multiple valid strategies, variable execution speed, or non-monotonic subgoals could induce misleading rewards. The paper discusses back-and-forth motions, but does not empirically stress-test such cases in depth.

The comparison to manually designed dense environment rewards is interesting but needs more care. Since Meta-World dense rewards are known to be imperfect and since TimeRewarder is combined with sparse success feedback and CLIP pretraining, outperforming those rewards should not be interpreted as generally surpassing hand-designed rewards.

Reproducibility is decent but not complete from the manuscript alone. Hyperparameters and protocols are listed, but code/data release status, exact preprocessing, human video collection details, sparse reward implementation, and adaptive alpha selection details could be specified more concretely to make the strong empirical claims easier to verify.
